name: Saudi Arabia

summary.text: The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is a monarchy on the Arabian Peninsula. Fifteen of the nineteen September 11, 2001 hijackers were Saudi nationals. The 9/11 Commission (2004) found no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior Saudi officials individually funded al Qaeda. A 28-page section of the 2002 congressional Joint Inquiry on possible Saudi links, declassified in July 2016, described unverified leads involving Omar al-Bayoumi and Fahad al-Thumairy. Under Executive Order 14040 (2021) the FBI released Operation Encore records, including a 2016 report describing assistance those two men gave two hijackers. The Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act became law over a presidential veto in September 2016, and on August 28, 2025 Judge George B. Daniels denied Saudi Arabia's renewed motion to dismiss the consolidated 9/11 families' lawsuit in the Southern District of New York. Saudi Arabia denies any role in the attacks.

facts.claim: Fifteen of the nineteen hijackers in the September 11, 2001 attacks were Saudi nationals, according to the 9/11 Commission's final report and subsequent reporting on the declassified congressional material.
facts.quote: Fifteen of the 19 hijackers were Saudi nationals, and several had little experience living in the West.

facts.claim: The 9/11 Commission's final report (July 2004) stated that Saudi Arabia had long been considered the primary source of al Qaeda funding, but that the Commission had found no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior Saudi officials individually funded the organization. The report also described Saudi Arabia as a place where al Qaeda raised money directly from individuals and through charities, and noted that charities with significant Saudi government sponsorship may have diverted funding to al Qaeda.
facts.quote: Saudi Arabia has long been considered the primary source of Al Qaeda funding, but we have found no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior Saudi officials individually funded the organization.

facts.claim: On the two Saudi nationals in California later central to the litigation, the 9/11 Commission wrote that it had seen no credible evidence that Omar al-Bayoumi believed in violent extremism or knowingly aided extremist groups, and that after exploring the available leads it had not found evidence that Fahad al-Thumairy provided assistance to hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar.
facts.quote: We have seen no credible evidence that he (Bayoumi) believed in violent extremism or knowingly aided extremists groups. ... After exploring the available leads, we have not found evidence that Thumairy provided assistance to the two operatives.

facts.claim: On July 15, 2016, the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence published the declassified 28-page section of the 2002 Joint Congressional Inquiry on possible foreign support for the hijackers, which had been withheld in full when the Inquiry's report was released in 2003. Chairman Devin Nunes stated that the section does not put forward vetted conclusions but unverified leads that were later fully investigated by the intelligence community.
facts.quote: this section does not put forward vetted conclusions, but rather unverified leads that were later fully investigated by the Intelligence Community.

sources.title: Intel Committee publishes declassified "28 pages"
'28 pages': Congress releases report on alleged Saudi 9/11 ties

facts.claim: The declassified 28 pages state that while in the United States some of the September 11 hijackers were in contact with, and received support or assistance from, individuals who may be connected to the Saudi government, and that Saudi government officials in the United States may have other ties to al Qaeda. They describe Omar al-Bayoumi as a U.S. resident who may have been a Saudi intelligence agent, with extensive contacts with Saudi officials and money from a Saudi defense contractor, and Fahad al-Thumairy as a Saudi consular official in Los Angeles and imam of a mosque two hijackers visited. The Joint Inquiry made no final determination on the reliability of the information.
facts.quote: While in the United States, some of the September 11 hijackers were in contact with, and received support or assistance from, individuals who may be connected to the Saudi Government

facts.claim: Responding to the declassification of the 28 pages in July 2016, Saudi Ambassador Abdullah Al-Saud said that the 9/11 Commission and several government agencies, including the CIA and the FBI, had investigated the contents of the pages and confirmed that neither the Saudi government, nor senior Saudi officials, nor any person acting on behalf of the Saudi government provided any support or encouragement for the attacks.
facts.quote: the 9/11 Commission and several government agencies, including the CIA and the FBI, have investigated the contents of the '28 Pages' and have confirmed that neither the Saudi government, nor senior Saudi officials, nor any person acting on behalf of the Saudi government provided any support or encouragement for these attacks.

facts.claim: Executive Order 14040 (September 3, 2021) directed a declassification review of documents on the September 11 attacks. On September 11, 2021 the FBI released the first document, a 16-page electronic communication dated April 4, 2016 summarizing its Operation Encore investigation, previously withheld in full in the litigation. Reporting on it said it describes al-Bayoumi as deeply involved in providing travel assistance, lodging and financing to two hijackers, and says al-Thumairy tasked an associate to help them and called them two very significant people. By December 2021 the FBI said more than 400 documents had been released and the review was ongoing.
facts.quote: an electronic communication dated April 4, 2016, from the subfile investigation described in chapter V of the 2015 Report of the Congressionally-directed 9/11 Review Commission to the Director of the FBI. This electronic communication had previously been withheld in full in the associated litigation.

facts.claim: A heavily redacted FBI memo from 2017, declassified under Executive Order 14040 and reported by CBS News, states that al-Bayoumi received a monthly payment as a cooptee of Saudi General Intelligence routed through then-Ambassador Prince Bandar bin Sultan, and that the earlier allegations about his Saudi intelligence ties were not confirmed at the time of the 9/11 Commission Report. A separate declassified FBI memo assessed, on the basis of source reporting, a 50/50 chance that al-Bayoumi had advance knowledge of the attacks. These are FBI assessments, not findings of fact.
facts.quote: the earlier allegations about his Saudi intelligence ties were not confirmed at the time of the 9/11 Commission Report. The above information confirms these allegations.

facts.claim: The FBI's Operation Encore records released under Executive Order 14040 describe the investigation as a casefile split off from the PENTTBOM investigation whose main subjects were Fahad al-Thumairy, Omar al-Bayoumi and Musaed al-Jarrah, and its closing material states that the evidence did not establish that the three knowingly conspired to assist the al Qaeda hijackers in furtherance of the attack.
facts.quote: the evidence did not establish that Thumairy, Bayoumi, and Al-Jarrah knowingly conspired to assist the AQ hijackers in furtherance of the 9/11 attack.

facts.claim: In 2024, evidence unsealed in the 9/11 families' lawsuit included a video, seized from al-Bayoumi's Birmingham home in 2001, showing him touring Washington, D.C. and filming the Capitol's architecture, entrances and security guards while referring to a plan; ProPublica reported that the FBI had not shared a full copy with its own field agents or the families, and that British police provided the full recording to the plaintiffs. Attorneys for Saudi Arabia described it as a tourist video and said a notepad sketch of a plane appeared to be a high school math assignment belonging to al-Bayoumi's child.
facts.quote: attorneys for the kingdom dismissed the Capitol "casing" film as a "tourist video that includes footage of artwork, flowerbeds, and a squirrel on the White House lawn."

facts.claim: The Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (S. 2040), which narrows foreign sovereign immunity for cases involving terrorist attacks on U.S. soil and allowed the 9/11 families to sue Saudi Arabia, became law on September 28, 2016 when the Senate voted 97-1 and the House 348-77 to override President Obama's veto, the first override of his presidency.
facts.quote: The Senate voted 97-1, and the House followed the same day, 348-77.

facts.claim: On August 28, 2025, Judge George B. Daniels of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York denied Saudi Arabia's renewed motion to dismiss the consolidated 9/11 families' claims (In re Terrorist Attacks on September 11, 2001), finding that the plaintiffs' allegations met the jurisdictional requirements of JASTA and that the evidence supported a reasonable inference that al-Bayoumi's and al-Thumairy's employment was more than their official job titles suggested. Judge Daniels had dismissed the claims in 2015 under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act before JASTA was enacted. The ruling allows the case to proceed; it is not a finding of liability.
facts.quote: Saudi Arabia's explanations were "either self-contradictory or not strong enough to overcome the inference that" the Kingdom had employed two individuals, Omar al-Bayoumi and Fahad al-Thumairy, to assist the hijackers.

In re Terrorist Attacks on September 11, 2001, MDL No. 1570 (docket)

facts.claim: Saudi Arabia has denied any role in the attacks. In the litigation its counsel argued that the plaintiffs' evidence did not show Saudi agents directly and knowingly helped the hijackers, and at a July 2024 hearing its lawyer Michael Kellogg argued that any help from al-Bayoumi was limited and wholly innocent; the embassy has stated that no evidence has ever emerged to indicate that the Saudi government or its officials had previous knowledge of the attack or were involved in its planning or execution.
facts.quote: No evidence has ever emerged to indicate that the Saudi government or its officials had previous knowledge of the terrorist attack or were in any way involved in its planning or execution

facts.claim: On October 14, 1973, Secretary of State Kissinger wrote to King Faisal that the United States had no alternative but to begin an airlift of supplies to Israel. A CIA Office of Economic Research memorandum of October 19, 1973 reported that Saudi Arabia had reportedly already cut production by 10 percent and that Libya, Abu Dhabi, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia had announced or threatened a total embargo against the United States, which then received about 1.6 million barrels a day of Arab oil.
facts.quote: Saudi Arabia has reportedly already cut current production by 10%

facts.claim: The State Department's Office of the Historian records that the 1973-74 embargo was imposed by Arab OPEC members against the United States in retaliation for the U.S. decision to resupply the Israeli military, that it banned petroleum exports to targeted countries and introduced production cuts, and that on November 7, 1973 the Nixon administration announced Project Independence. Secondary accounts date the Saudi cutoff of exports to the United States to October 19-20, 1973, following the administration's request for $2.2 billion in aid to Israel.
facts.quote: imposed by Arab OPEC members against the United States in retaliation for the U.S. decision to re-supply the Israeli military

facts.claim: On November 26, 1973, Ambassador Akins reported from Jidda that Prince Fahd said Saudi Arabia was prepared to ease the boycott on the United States and resume production provided the Arabs could see concrete steps toward a just peace in the Middle East.
facts.quote: prepared to ease the boycott on the U.S. and resume production provided the Arabs can see concrete steps being taken toward a just peace in the Middle East

facts.claim: In March 1974 the State Department instructed the embassy in Jidda to approach the Saudis promptly at a high level, suggesting Prince Fahd, about joint commissions for cooperation in economic, military/strategic and scientific fields, to offer an alternative to European arrangements trading technology for guaranteed oil supply. The embassy reported the Saudi reaction as uniformly enthusiastic, with a consensus that Fahd should head the Saudi side and a Saudi insistence on secrecy until simultaneous announcement in Washington and Riyadh.
facts.quote: the Saudis also insisted that the matter be kept secret until officially announced simultaneously in Washington and Riyadh.

facts.claim: The U.S.-Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation was established under a joint communique of June 8, 1974 signed by Secretary of State Kissinger and Prince Fahd, co-chaired by the U.S. Treasury Secretary and the Saudi Minister of Finance and National Economy. GAO reported in March 1979 that it provided U.S. technical assistance to the Saudi government on a fully reimbursable basis, funded almost entirely from the Saudi Arabian Trust Account in the U.S. Treasury, with sixteen project agreements worth about $800 million under way as of September 1978 and about 133 U.S. technicians in Saudi Arabia.
facts.quote: The Commission was established under a Joint Communique signed June 8, 1974 (Signed by Secretary of State Kissenger and Prince Fahad of Saudi Arabia)

facts.claim: On August 27, 1974 the U.S. embassy in Jidda reported that Oil Minister Yamani said U.S. approaches on oil prices from April through July had been discussed at length in the Saudi Cabinet and accepted, and that the Cabinet had agreed Saudi Arabia must hold the line against any price increase at the September OPEC meeting, where Iran demanded a 35 percent rise.
facts.quote: The Cabinet had agreed that at the OPEC meeting the end of September Saudi Arabia must hold the line against any price increase.

facts.claim: In April 1975 Ambassador Akins wrote that Saudi Arabia had already agreed that year to place enough funds in U.S. Treasury notes and FNMA issues to cover more than half of the U.S. balance-of-payments deficit. GAO reported in 1979 that the Treasury's noncompetitive 'add-on' facility for buying Treasury securities outside the auctions had first been offered to Saudi Arabia and that Treasury had made special commitments of financial confidentiality to Saudi Arabia.
facts.quote: Saudi Arabia has already agreed this year to place enough in Treasury notes and FNMA issues to cover more than half our balance of payment deficit.

openQuestions: The site's claim that the attack was 'misattributed to the wrong party' is not what the record shows: every official finding attributes the attacks to al Qaeda, and the open question in the sources is whether Saudi officials or employees knowingly assisted two hijackers. The 9/11 Commission (2004) found no evidence of institutional or senior-official funding; the FBI's Encore closing material says the evidence did not establish a knowing conspiracy by al-Bayoumi, al-Thumairy and al-Jarrah; the August 2025 SDNY ruling finds only that the plaintiffs' evidence is enough to proceed to trial. No source connects any Saudi role to a decision to invade Iraq.

The exact text and page numbers of the 9/11 Commission quotes were taken from secondary reporting that reproduces them; the owner should confirm them against the GovInfo PDF (chapter 5 for the funding finding, chapter 7 for al-Bayoumi and al-Thumairy).

The 2017 FBI memo describing al-Bayoumi as a 'cooptee of Saudi General Intelligence' and the Encore closing statement are cited through CBS News and the FBI Vault release page; the specific Vault document containing each passage was not identified in this session.

The August 28, 2025 opinion itself was not retrieved; the quotations come from CNN and a legal blog. The CourtListener docket for MDL 1570 is cited for locating the order. Reporting in 2025 also says Saudi Arabia faces further appellate proceedings over discovery.

The site's crash-conduits node names 'Riggs Bank' accounts wiring funds to facilitators and 'CIA Alec Station' withholding intelligence; neither was researched here. The CIA Inspector General's 2007 executive summary (recorded under cia.json) addresses the watchlisting failure without any finding of intent.

Fact-checkers note the Commission's finding is narrow (state institutions and senior officials acting individually) and that commissioners Gorelick and Lehman later said Saudi individuals, possibly including lower-level officials, likely helped; those statements were not recorded as facts.

The Saudi announcement halting exports to the United States is usually dated October 20, 1973 (some accounts say October 19 or 21). The FRUS telegram reporting the announcement itself was not surfaced; the nearest primary document found is the CIA memorandum of October 19 (FRUS vol. XXXVI Doc. 223), which describes the total embargo as announced or threatened. The owner should locate the Jidda telegram in the volume's October 1973 run (Documents 209-344).

No document found states a Saudi commitment to price oil only in dollars in exchange for U.S. protection; the 1974 records (Joint Commission communique, Treasury securities purchases, add-on facility, confidentiality) do not contain such a clause, and a July 2024 Radio Free Asia fact check found no known formal deal of that kind. See the saudi-arabian-monetary-agency record for the sources.
